claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Weiss et al., 2016

claims.claim: Part of the central metabolism of T. ammonificans is ancestral and emerged prior to oxygenic photosynthesis.
claims.source: Taken together, these observations suggest that part of the central metabolism of T. ammonificans is ancestral and emerged prior to oxygenic photosynthesis.
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparative genomic analysis and metabolic reconstruction

claims.claim: The monomeric napA gene of T. ammonificans is homologous to that of Desulfovibrio desulfuricans and other Deltaproteobacteria and apparently has been acquired laterally.
claims.source: The monomeric napA gene of T. ammonificans is homologous to that of Desulfovibrio desulfuricans and other Deltaproteobacteria (Figure 6; online interactive version) and apparently has been acquired laterally.
claims.evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis shown in Figure 6

claims.claim: The napA gene of T. ammonificans shares high similarity with assimilatory nitrate reductases (Nas) and could be an evolutionary intermediate form between assimilatory Nas and the dimeric respiratory Nap.

claims.evidence: Inferred from sequence similarity analysis

claims.claim: Group 1 Hyn hydrogenases are linked through the membrane quinone pool to nitrate reduction in T. ammonificans.
claims.source: Based on the finding that Group 1 Hyn hydrogenases were expressed when T. ammonificans was grown under nitrate-reducing conditions (Figure 3), we suggest that these enzymes are linked through the membrane quinone pool to nitrate reduction and may have been acquired simultaneously with the nap genes.
claims.evidence: Inferred from proteomic data shown in Figure 3

claims.claim: Oxygen-stress related genes in T. ammonificans are not part of the core, or ancestral genome, but evolved as a response to exposure to toxic oxygen radicals.
claims.source: We propose that such genes are not part of the core, or ancestral genome of T. ammonificans, but that they evolved as a response to exposure to toxic oxygen radicals.
claims.evidence: Proposed based on comparative genomic analysis and evolutionary inference

claims.claim: The nitrate reduction pathway and oxygen stress-related genes may represent adaptations acquired by the T. ammonificans lineage to cope with the rise of oxygen on Earth.
claims.source: In conclusion, the nitrate reduction pathway, as well as oxygen stress-related genes, may represent adaptations acquired by the T. ammonificans lineage to cope with the rise of oxygen on Earth.
claims.evidence: Proposed based on comparative genomic analysis and evolutionary inference

claims.claim: The reductive acetyl-CoA pathway is present in acetogenic bacteria, methanogens, sulfate-reducers and anammox bacteria.

claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Berg et al., 2010

claims.claim: The key enzyme of the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway is the bifunctional heterotetramer enzyme carbon monoxide dehydrogenase/acetyl-CoA synthase (CODH/ACS).

claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Berg et al., 2010 and established knowledge

claims.claim: Sequence analysis of the T. ammonificans CodH protein sequence revealed the presence of conserved residues necessary for the interaction with Acs and for the coordination of the NiFeS cluster.

claims.evidence: Based on sequence analysis

claims.claim: The type V CodH may catalyze the reduction of CO2 to CO.
claims.source: We hypothesize that the type V CodH, which, based on structural and size considerations may represent the most ancestral version of this class of enzymes (Frank Robb, personal communication), may catalyze the reduction of CO2 to CO.
claims.evidence: Proposed based on structural considerations and inference

claims.claim: Within the Aquificae, the type V CodH is exclusive to the Desulfurobacteriaceae.

claims.evidence: Inferred from comparative genomic analysis

claims.claim: The reductive acetyl-CoA pathway could be operational in T. ammonificans in addition to the rTCA cycle.

claims.evidence: Inferred from proteomic data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—source data 1

claims.claim: The use of different carbon fixation strategies could be advantageous under energy limiting conditions, could optimize overall carbon fixation or provide different precursors for biosynthetic pathways.

claims.evidence: Proposed based on inference from metabolic analysis

claims.claim: The presence of a reductive acetyl-CoA pathway in T. ammonificans and other members of the Desulfurobacteriaceae supports the scenario that a complete and operational reductive acetyl-CoA pathway was present in the ancestor of the phylum Aquificae.
claims.source: Furthermore, this finding supports the scenario proposed by Braakman and Smith that a complete and operational reductive acetyl-CoA pathway was present in the ancestor of the phylum Aquificae (Braakman and Smith, 2012).
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparative genomic analysis and supported by citation to Braakman and Smith, 2012

claims.claim: The rise of oxygen has been interpreted as one of the factors responsible for the diversification of carbon fixation from the ancestral pathway.

claims.evidence: Inferred from comparative genomic analysis with reference to Table 2

claims.claim: A complete rTCA cycle could have evolved in the Aquificaceae from an ancestral, incomplete version of the cycle.
claims.source: Since citryl-CoA synthetase and 2-oxoglutarate carboxylase likely evolved by duplication of the genes for the succinyl-CoA synthetase and pyruvate carboxylase (Aoshima, 2007; Braakman and Smith, 2012), a complete rTCA cycle could have evolved in the Aquificaceae from an ancestral, incomplete version of the cycle.
claims.evidence: Inferred from evolutionary analysis with citations to Aoshima, 2007 and Braakman and Smith, 2012

claims.claim: Temperature may have played a role in preserving the ancient, more symmetric, two-step citrate cleavage rTCA cycle variant in Aquificaceae.

claims.evidence: Proposed based on inference from comparative analysis shown in Figure 10

claims.claim: Members of Aquificaceae have optimum growth temperatures (75–95°C) higher than those of the two other groups (60–75°C).
claims.source: Members of this group have optimum growth temperatures (75–95°C) higher than those of the two other groups (60–75°C; Table 1), and the 'ancient' enzymes might be more stable at these high temperatures.
claims.evidence: Based on data from Table 1

claims.claim: The 'newer' enzymes that catalyze the one-step citrate cleavage might have evolved to function optimally at lower temperatures.
claims.source: In contrast, the 'newer' enzymes that catalyze the one-step citrate cleavage might have evolved to function optimally at lower temperatures.
claims.evidence: Proposed based on inference from temperature and enzyme evolution

claims.claim: All the extant members of the Aquificae phylum possess the genes encoding for the enzymes of the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway, with the exception of codH (encoding for the CO-dehydrogenase), which is only found in the Desulfurobacteriaceae.
claims.source: Different members of the Aquificae use either one of the two versions of the rTCA cycle, and all the extant members of this phylum possess the genes encoding for the enzymes of the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway, with the exception of codH (encoding for the CO-dehydrogenase), which is only found in the Desulfurobacteriaceae.
claims.evidence: Based on comparative genomic analysis

claims.claim: The last common ancestor of the Aquificae combined the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway with an incomplete form of the rTCA that did not proceed past the synthesis of 2-oxoglutarate.
claims.source: Alltogether, our results suggest that the last common ancestor of the Aquificae combined the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway with an incomplete form of the rTCA that did not proceed past the synthesis of 2-oxoglutarate (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: Inferred from integrated phylogenetic and comparative genomic analyses shown in Figure 10

claims.claim: An incomplete version of the rTCA pathway, consisting only of the reactions from acetyl-CoA to 2-oxoglutarate, is present in extant methanogens.
claims.source: A similar incomplete version of the rTCA pathway, consisting only of the reactions from acetyl-CoA to 2-oxoglutarate, is present in extant methanogens (Berg, 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Berg, 2011

claims.claim: The phylometabolic reconstruction of the ancestral state of carbon fixation in the Aquificae is conceptually consistent with chemoautotrophic processes of extant Bacteria and Archaea, and may represent the earliest carbon fixation pathway.
claims.source: Thus, our phylometabolic reconstruction of the ancestral state of carbon fixation in the Aquificae (Figure 10) is conceptually consistent with chemoautotrophic processes of extant Bacteria and Archaea, and may represent the earliest carbon fixation pathway.
claims.evidence: Proposed based on phylometabolic reconstruction shown in Figure 10

results.result: T. ammonificans belongs to the deep-branching phylum Aquificae, whose cultured members are thermophilic chemolithoautotrophs that use hydrogen as an energy source, grow optimally at 65-95°C, and rely on the rTCA cycle for carbon fixation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are well-supported by multiple citations to prior work (Lebedinsky et al., 2007; Sievert and Vetriani, 2012; Di Giulio, 2003; Pitulle et al., 1994; Battistuzzi et al., 2004; Hügler et al., 2007; Hügler and Sievert, 2011) and reference to phylogenetic data (Figure 1, Table 1). These claims establish the phylogenetic and physiological context for the study organism.

results.result: The T. ammonificans HB-1 genome consists of a 1,682,965 bp chromosome and a 76,561 bp plasmid, encoding 1890 genes (1831 protein-coding), with 75.16% assigned putative functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8 describe basic genome characteristics supported by prior publication (Giovannelli et al., 2012) and Figure 2. These are straightforward genomic descriptors that provide foundational information for subsequent analyses.

results.result: Proteomic analysis identified 780 proteins (43% of predicted ORFs) in T. ammonificans grown under nitrate-reducing conditions, with rTCA cycle enzymes comprising 6% and reductive acetyl-CoA pathway enzymes comprising 1.25% of identified proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11 are supported by proteomic data (Figure 3, Figure 3—source data 1, Table 2). The proteomic coverage is reasonable (43%), and the relative abundances provide quantitative evidence for pathway activity. The lower abundance of acetyl-CoA pathway enzymes compared to rTCA enzymes is a key observation.

results.result: The rTCA cycle is widespread among anaerobic and microaerophilic bacteria, while the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway is believed to be the most ancient carbon fixation pathway on Earth.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13 are well-supported by citations to established literature (Berg, 2011; Fuchs, 2011; Hügler and Sievert, 2011). These are background claims about the distribution and evolutionary significance of carbon fixation pathways.

results.result: T. ammonificans encodes a type V CodH (87% similar to D. thermolithotrophum) with conserved residues for Acs interaction and NiFeS cluster coordination, which may represent the most ancestral version of this enzyme class and is exclusive to Desulfurobacteriaceae within Aquificae.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C18, C66-C68 describe the type V CodH. While the sequence analysis (C66) and comparative genomics (C17, C18) are supported by data, the claims about ancestral nature (C16) and catalytic function (C67) are speculative, based on personal communication and structural inference without experimental validation. The phylogenetic exclusivity to Desulfurobacteriaceae (C68) is inferred but not rigorously tested. The function of type V CodH remains experimentally unconfirmed.

results.result: The detection of CodH and formate dehydrogenase in the proteome suggests the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway could be operational in T. ammonificans alongside the rTCA cycle, potentially providing metabolic flexibility under energy-limiting conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 propose dual carbon fixation pathways. While proteomic detection of key enzymes (C69) provides some support, the pathway is incomplete (missing 10-formyl-THF synthetase), and no functional assays demonstrate actual CO2 fixation via this route. The proposed advantages (C70) are speculative. The connection to ancestral Aquificae metabolism (C71) is inferential.

results.result: T. ammonificans uses the Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas pathway for gluconeogenesis, with the fbp gene present in some but not all Aquificae genomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20 are supported by genome analysis identifying key genes and comparative genomics showing differential distribution of fbp across Aquificae. The presence/absence pattern is clearly documented with citations (Deckert et al., 1998).

results.result: T. ammonificans Group 1 hydrogenases (Hyn) are more similar to Deltaproteobacteria than to other Aquificae, suggesting lateral gene transfer of the hydrogen oxidation/nitrate reduction respiratory pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C24 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 5) and comparative genomics showing closer similarity to Deltaproteobacteria than to Aquificae relatives. The inference of horizontal gene transfer (C23) is reasonable given the phylogenetic incongruence, though the direction and timing are not definitively established.

results.result: T. ammonificans and D. thermolithotrophum possess both Group 3a and 3b cytoplasmic hydrogenases, which have polyphyletic origins, with Group 2 hydrogenases found only in microaerobes and Group 3a in strict anaerobes.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C28 are supported by genome analysis (C25, citation to Jeon et al., 2015) and phylogenetic analysis (Figure 5) showing polyphyletic origins (C26). The correlation between hydrogenase groups and oxygen tolerance (C27-C28) is supported by comparative genomic data across multiple organisms.

results.result: T. ammonificans reduces nitrate to ammonium using a unique monomeric periplasmic nitrate reductase (lacking NapB) with an operon structure similar to Deltaproteobacteria, distinct from other Aquificae.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C32 are supported by prior physiological characterization (Vetriani et al., 2004), genome/proteome analysis (Figure 3), and comparative genomics (Vetriani et al., 2014; Jepson et al., 2006). The unique operon structure and monomeric nature are well-documented.

results.result: T. ammonificans reduces elemental sulfur to hydrogen sulfide, though the pathway remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claim C33 is supported by prior physiological characterization (Vetriani et al., 2004). The acknowledgment that the pathway is unclear is appropriate given the uncertainty about the specific enzymes involved.

results.result: Despite being a strict anaerobe, T. ammonificans encodes oxygen radical detoxification genes including catalase/peroxidase, superoxide reductase, cytochrome-C peroxidase, and cytochrome bd complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 are supported by genome analysis (Figure 3), prior enzyme activity detection (Vetriani et al., 2004), and citations about cytochrome bd function (Das et al., 2005; Mason et al., 2009). The apparent paradox of oxygen defense genes in an anaerobe is well-documented.

results.result: T. ammonificans possesses one to two terminal flagella.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 is supported by prior characterization (Vetriani et al., 2004). This is a straightforward morphological observation.

results.result: 34% of T. ammonificans coding sequences share higher similarity to genes outside the Aquificae, indicating extensive horizontal gene transfer.
results.evaluation: Claim C38 is supported by comparative genomic analysis (Figure 6). The 34% figure represents substantial genomic mosaicism, though the specific methodology for determining 'higher similarity' could be more explicitly described.

results.result: Dual carbon fixation pathways have been confirmed only in the Riftia pachyptila endosymbiont, which can switch between CBB and rTCA cycles in response to energy availability.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 are supported by citation to Markert et al., 2007. These provide context for the proposed dual pathway in T. ammonificans by citing a precedent.

results.result: Aquificaceae use the two-step (symmetric) rTCA cycle variant, while Hydrogenothermaceae and Desulfurobacteriaceae use the one-step (asymmetric) variant, with ATP citrate lyase likely acquired by the latter two families through horizontal gene transfer.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C49 are supported by comparative genomic analysis (Figures 8-9), phylogenetic analysis (Figure 9), and multiple citations (Aoshima et al., 2004; Braakman and Smith, 2012; Hügler et al., 2007). The phylogenetic evidence that ACL in Hydrogenothermaceae and Desulfurobacteriaceae is more similar to Nitrospira/Chlorobia than to Aquificaceae supports the HGT inference (C44-C45). The presence of ccl in Hydrogenothermaceae (C47) and its absence in Desulfurobacteriaceae (C49) are clearly documented.

results.result: The last common ancestor of Aquificae possessed the complete reductive acetyl-CoA pathway combined with an incomplete rTCA cycle (not proceeding past 2-oxoglutarate synthesis), with Desulfurobacteriaceae retaining CodH due to anaerobic lifestyle while microaerophilic families lost it.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52, C78 represent the central evolutionary reconstruction. While supported by comparative genomics and phylogenetic analyses (Figure 10), this is an inference based on parsimony rather than direct evidence. The incomplete rTCA in the ancestor (C50) is inferred from gene distribution patterns. The retention/loss of CodH correlated with oxygen tolerance (C52) is a reasonable inference but not definitively proven. Alternative evolutionary scenarios are not rigorously excluded.

results.result: The Aquificae ancestor was a hydrogen-oxidizing, sulfur-reducing bacterium using a hybrid carbon fixation pathway, which acquired genes for metabolic flexibility (e.g., nitrate respiration) in response to rising atmospheric oxygen while retaining ancestral traits.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 represent the overarching evolutionary narrative. While conceptually consistent with the data, these are speculative reconstructions. The hybrid pathway in the ancestor (C53) is inferred but not proven. The connection to oxygen rise (C54) is plausible but circumstantial. The claim that T. ammonificans represents a 'modern analog' of early metabolism (C55) and that pathway redundancy was common in ancestral organisms (C56) are interesting hypotheses but lack direct supporting evidence.

results.result: Part of T. ammonificans central metabolism is ancestral and emerged prior to oxygenic photosynthesis, consistent with LUCA being a hydrogen-dependent autotroph using the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 connect the findings to LUCA reconstruction (Weiss et al., 2016). While the consistency with LUCA models (C57) is noted, the inference that T. ammonificans metabolism is ancestral and pre-dates oxygenic photosynthesis (C58) is speculative. The presence of genes for oxygen-sensitive pathways does not definitively prove they are ancestral rather than convergently evolved.

results.result: The monomeric napA gene was laterally acquired from Deltaproteobacteria and may represent an evolutionary intermediate between assimilatory and respiratory nitrate reductases, with Group 1 Hyn hydrogenases linked to nitrate reduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 are supported by comparative genomics (Figure 6) and proteomic data (Figure 3). The lateral acquisition (C59) is well-supported by phylogenetic incongruence. The proposal that napA is an evolutionary intermediate (C60) is speculative but reasonable given sequence similarities. The linkage of Hyn to nitrate reduction (C61) is inferred from co-expression but not functionally validated.

results.result: Oxygen stress-related genes and the nitrate reduction pathway represent adaptations acquired to cope with rising atmospheric oxygen rather than ancestral traits.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 propose that oxygen defense and nitrate respiration are acquired rather than ancestral. While the phylogenetic evidence for lateral transfer of nitrate reduction genes is strong, the inference that oxygen defense genes are not ancestral (C62) is speculative. The correlation with oxygen rise (C63) is plausible but not definitively proven—these genes could have other functions or evolutionary origins.

results.result: The reductive acetyl-CoA pathway is present in acetogens, methanogens, sulfate-reducers, and anammox bacteria, with CODH/ACS as the key bifunctional enzyme.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 are well-supported by citation to Berg et al., 2010 and established knowledge. These provide background on the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway.

results.result: The rise of oxygen drove diversification of carbon fixation pathways, with the complete rTCA cycle potentially evolving in Aquificaceae from an ancestral incomplete version through gene duplication.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 propose oxygen as a driver of pathway evolution. While the correlation between oxygen tolerance and CodH loss is noted (C72), the causal relationship is inferred. The evolution of the complete rTCA through gene duplication (C73) is supported by citations (Aoshima, 2007; Braakman and Smith, 2012) but remains inferential.

results.result: Temperature may have preserved the ancient two-step rTCA variant in high-temperature Aquificaceae (75-95°C), while newer one-step enzymes evolved for optimal function at lower temperatures (60-75°C).
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 propose temperature as a factor in enzyme evolution. While the temperature differences are documented (C75, Table 1), the hypothesis that temperature drove enzyme retention/evolution (C74, C76) is speculative without experimental validation of enzyme thermostability or activity optima.

results.result: All extant Aquificae possess genes for the reductive acetyl-CoA pathway except codH, which is exclusive to Desulfurobacteriaceae.
results.evaluation: Claim C77 is supported by comprehensive comparative genomic analysis across Aquificae genomes (Table 2, Table 3). This is a key observation for the evolutionary reconstruction.

results.result: An incomplete rTCA pathway (acetyl-CoA to 2-oxoglutarate) exists in extant methanogens.
results.evaluation: Claim C79 is supported by citation to Berg, 2011. This provides a modern analog for the proposed ancestral incomplete rTCA in Aquificae.

results.result: The phylometabolic reconstruction of ancestral Aquificae carbon fixation is consistent with extant chemoautotrophic processes and may represent the earliest carbon fixation pathway.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 represents the culminating conclusion. While the reconstruction is conceptually consistent with known pathways, the claim that it 'may represent the earliest carbon fixation pathway' is highly speculative. The phylometabolic approach provides a plausible hypothesis but cannot definitively establish what the earliest pathway was.
